name: Nepal
tagline: Newar cities, Sherpa trails, the walled north
meta_description: Plan Nepal from India or abroad: Kathmandu valley cities, Pokhara, Everest and Annapurna treks, Mustang, real costs in INR, permits and altitude advice.
summary: Nepal is the easiest big Himalayan trip for Indians: no visa, an open land border, the rupee pegged at 1 INR = 1.6 NPR. Come for the Newar cities of the Kathmandu valley, the lake town of Pokhara, teahouse treks to Poon Hill and Everest Base Camp, and the walled town of Lo Manthang. October–November and March–April are best.
intro: We call Nepal a hive of hives. In one country you move from the brick courtyards of the Kathmandu valley, where Newar families have cast bronze and set curd in clay pots for centuries, to Gurung villages above Pokhara, Thakali apple orchards in the Kali Gandaki, Sherpa lodges under Everest and the Tibetan-speaking walled town of Lo Manthang. The distances are short on the map and long on the road: Kathmandu to Pokhara is about 200 km and still takes 7–8 hours by bus.

For Indian travellers Nepal is unusually simple. There is no visa, you can cross on foot at Sunauli or Raxaul with a passport or voter ID, and the Nepali rupee has been pegged to the Indian rupee at 1.6 NPR for 1 INR since 1993. Indian ₹100 notes are taken almost everywhere. Larger notes were restricted for years; in 2026 Nepal Rastra Bank allowed post-2016 ₹200 and ₹500 notes up to ₹25,000 per person. Check current status before you travel.

International visitors get a visa on arrival at Tribhuvan International Airport and the main land borders: in 2026 it costs USD 30 for 15 days, USD 50 for 30 days and USD 125 for 90 days. Most trips start in Kathmandu, add Bhaktapur and Patan as day trips or overnights, then go west to Pokhara for the Annapurna foothills or fly to Lukla for the Khumbu. Upper Mustang needs a restricted-area permit and a licensed guide.

We plan Nepal at three price levels. Saver trips use tourist buses, teahouses and simple guesthouses and can be done for ₹2,000–3,500 a day in the cities and hills. Comfort trips add a private car, good hotels such as Temple Tree in Pokhara and heritage stays like The Old Inn at Bandipur. Signature trips use Dwarika's in Kathmandu, Tiger Mountain Pokhara Lodge and the Mountain Lodges of Nepal chain on the Everest trail.

story.title: A valley that was a lake, a road to Tibet

chapters.heading: The lake Manjushri drained
chapters.text: The Swayambhu Purana tells that the Kathmandu valley was once a lake, and that the bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gorge at Chobhar with his sword so people could reach the light shining from a lotus at Swayambhu. Geologists agree on the lake, if not the sword: the valley floor is old lake sediment, which is why it is so flat and so fertile. On that soil the Newar people built three rival royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, each with a Durbar Square of temples and palace courtyards. The valley's monuments were inscribed together on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1979 as seven monument zones.

chapters.heading: Salt, wool and the Newar merchants
chapters.text: For centuries Nepal lived off trade between India and Tibet. Salt and wool came south over high passes; grain, cloth and metalwork went north. Newar merchants from the valley ran trading houses as far as Lhasa, and Boudhanath grew up as a halt on the Tibet road. When Prithvi Narayan Shah conquered the valley in 1768, Newar traders from Bhaktapur moved west and founded Bandipur as a stop on the India–Tibet route. In the 1770s the King of Kaski brought sixteen Newar families from Bhaktapur to set up the market at Pokhara. Their brick houses with carved windows still line both bazaars.

chapters.heading: Thakali, Gurung, Sherpa
chapters.text: Away from the valley, each hill people found its own living. The Thakali of the Kali Gandaki ran the salt trade and the inns along it, and when trade with Tibet faded they turned Marpha into Nepal's apple capital, making brandy and jam from the fruit. The Gurung villages above Pokhara, Ghandruk among them, sent generations of young men into the Gurkha regiments, and pensions built many of their stone houses. In the Khumbu the Sherpa people, whose ancestors crossed from Tibet, traded at the Saturday market in Namche Bazaar and later became the backbone of Himalayan mountaineering.

chapters.heading: The kingdom behind the wall
chapters.text: North of the main Himalayan crest lies Upper Mustang, the old Kingdom of Lo. Its capital, Lo Manthang, was founded in 1380 by Ame Pal and is still enclosed by a mud-brick wall. The region was closed to outsiders until 1992, which is one reason its painted gompas and cave shrines survived. The kings of Lo kept their title inside Nepal until the government ended the monarchy there on 7 October 2008; the last king, Jigme Dorje Palbar Bista, died in 2016. Every spring the town still holds Tiji, three days of masked dances in the palace square.

highlights.title: Three royal cities in one valley
highlights.text: Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur sit within 15 km of each other, each with its own Durbar Square, palace courtyards and pagoda temples. Patan is the city of metal casters, Bhaktapur of potters and juju dhau curd. Two days covers the main squares; three lets you walk the back lanes.

highlights.title: Teahouse treks without a tent
highlights.text: On Nepal's main trails you sleep and eat in family-run lodges called teahouses. A room costs ₹300–1,200 and dal bhat ₹400–900, rising with altitude. Poon Hill takes 4–5 days from Pokhara; Everest Base Camp takes 12–14 days from Kathmandu with acclimatisation.

highlights.title: Pokhara and the Annapurnas
highlights.text: Pokhara sits at about 800 m beside Phewa Lake, and within 30 km the land rises to peaks above 7,500 m. Machapuchare, the 6,993 m Fishtail, is closed to climbing for religious reasons. Dawn from Sarangkot and a boat across the lake are the two things not to miss.

highlights.title: Everest country and the Sherpa capital
highlights.text: A flight to Lukla and two days on foot bring you to Namche Bazaar at 3,440 m, with its Saturday market. Beyond lie Khumjung, where Hillary's Himalayan Trust built a school in 1961, and Tengboche monastery at 3,867 m, home of the Mani Rimdu festival.

highlights.title: Apples, wind and the Kali Gandaki
highlights.text: The Kali Gandaki valley between Jomsom and Marpha is dry, stony and famous for its afternoon wind. Thakali Marpha is Nepal's apple capital and sells local brandy and dried apple. Muktinath, at about 3,760 m, is holy to both Hindus and Buddhists and reachable by jeep.

highlights.title: Lo Manthang, the walled town
highlights.text: Upper Mustang was closed until 1992. Its capital Lo Manthang, founded in 1380, keeps its wall, palace and painted gompas such as Jampa Lhakhang. Since late 2025 foreigners pay USD 50 a day for the restricted-area permit and must travel with a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

budget.covers: Hostel or simple guesthouse, dal bhat and momos, tourist buses and shared jeeps; teahouse treks ₹3,000–4,500 a day with guide share
3–4 star or heritage hotel, private car with driver, domestic flights where useful, guide for sightseeing

money_savers: Carry Indian ₹100 notes or change money into NPR at the border; the peg is fixed at 1 INR = 1.6 NPR, so anyone offering much less is taking a cut.

Show your Indian passport or voter ID at heritage sites: SAARC visitors pay NPR 500 at Bhaktapur against NPR 1,800 for other foreigners, and similar discounts apply at Patan and Kathmandu Durbar Squares.
Take a tourist bus from Kathmandu to Pokhara for NPR 800–1,200 instead of a private car at ₹9,000–12,000; it takes the same 7–8 hours on the same road.
On treks, eat dal bhat: one order includes refills, and it costs less than pasta or pizza carried up by porter.
Carry a filter bottle or purification tablets and refill at lodges; bottled water rises from NPR 30 in Kathmandu to NPR 300–400 near Everest Base Camp.
Buy a Nepal Telecom or Ncell SIM with your passport on arrival; Indian roaming in Nepal is expensive and many Indian prepaid plans do not cover it.
getting_there: By air, Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport has direct flights from Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata and Varanasi, among others; Delhi to Kathmandu takes about 1 h 40 min. By road, most Indian travellers cross at Sunauli (from Gorakhpur, ≈ 95 km · 3 h) into Bhairahawa, then take a bus to Pokhara (≈ 180 km · 7–9 h) or Kathmandu (≈ 280 km · 8–10 h). From Bihar, cross at Raxaul into Birgunj and take a bus to Kathmandu (≈ 270 km · 7–9 h). Gautam Buddha International Airport at Bhairahawa and Pokhara International Airport (opened January 2023) also have some international flights. Inside Nepal, tourist buses link Kathmandu, Pokhara and Chitwan, and small planes fly to Lukla and Jomsom, weather permitting.
permits: Indian citizens need no visa; carry a valid passport or Election Commission voter ID (Aadhaar and PAN are not accepted for adults). Other nationalities get a visa on arrival (USD 30/50/125 for 15/30/90 days in 2026). Treks need park permits: Annapurna Conservation Area (NPR 1,000 SAARC, NPR 3,000 others), Sagarmatha National Park (NPR 1,500 SAARC, NPR 3,000 others) plus the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu municipality fee. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers in most parks must hire a licensed guide. Upper Mustang needs a restricted-area permit. Check current status before you travel.

months.summary: January is cold, dry and clear. The Kathmandu valley is at its sharpest for sightseeing, with frosty mornings and warm afternoons, though winter smog can blur the mountain view by midday. Pokhara is mild at 7–20 °C. High treks are possible but cold; many lodges above 4,000 m close and Upper Mustang largely empties as residents winter in the south. Low prices and few crowds make this a good month for the valley cities and Nagarkot sunrises.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket for Kathmandu evenings; many guesthouses have no central heating.

months.summary: February warms quickly and the skies stay mostly clear. It is a good month for the Kathmandu valley, Bandipur and Pokhara, and for low treks such as Poon Hill, where the snow at Ghorepani is beginning to melt. Sherpa Losar, the Tibetan-calendar new year, often falls in February in the Khumbu and Boudhanath. Higher passes remain snowbound. Hotel rates are still low, and Pokhara's lake is calm in the mornings.
months.tip: Check the Losar date for the year; Boudhanath fills with families and butter lamps.

months.summary: March opens the spring trekking season. Rhododendrons begin to flower on the Poon Hill ridge, the Everest trail fills from mid-month, and peak-season Lukla flights move to Ramechhap (Manthali) airport, about 4 hours by road from Kathmandu. Afternoon haze grows towards the end of the month, so mountain views are best early. Valley cities are pleasant, and Holi is celebrated in Kathmandu and Pokhara.
months.tip: Book Lukla flights early for late March and budget for the Ramechhap transfer.

months.summary: April is the busiest spring month. Rhododendron forests above Ghandruk and Ghorepani are in full flower, Everest Base Camp hosts the climbing expeditions, and Upper Mustang opens up. Bhaktapur's Bisket Jatra marks the Nepali new year in mid-April with chariot pulling and the raising of a tall pole at Yoshin Khel. Lowland heat builds and haze softens the views by late morning.
months.tip: Book Bhaktapur rooms for the Bisket Jatra nights well ahead.

months.summary: May is warm and hazy in the hills, with afternoon thunderstorms building from mid-month. It is a strong month for Upper Mustang, which lies in the rain shadow; Tiji fills Lo Manthang's palace square with masked dances, usually in May. The Everest summit season peaks, so Namche and the trail to base camp are busy. Valley cities are hot by midday; Nagarkot and Bandipur stay cooler.
months.tip: For Tiji, plan 10–13 days so you can acclimatise before the festival.

months.summary: The monsoon usually reaches Nepal in mid-June. Leeches appear on mid-altitude trails, roads see landslides, and Lukla flights are often cancelled. The exception is the rain-shadow north: Upper Mustang, Jomsom and Marpha stay mostly dry and green at the edges. Kathmandu is humid with heavy evening showers. Prices drop and the cities are quiet, but cloud hides most mountain views.
months.tip: Build a spare day into any monsoon itinerary for road or flight delays.

months.summary: July is the wettest month. The Kathmandu–Pokhara highway and roads to Jomsom can close for hours or days after landslides, and Pokhara records some of Nepal's highest rainfall. Upper Mustang remains the best trekking choice. In the valley, rice planting fills the terraces and the temples are uncrowded. Treat this as a culture month in the cities or a Mustang month, nothing in between.
months.tip: Carry a rain cover for your daypack and plastic sleeves for your passport.

months.summary: August is still monsoon, though the rain becomes patchier late in the month. The Newar festival calendar picks up: Gai Jatra in Kathmandu and Bhaktapur, and Krishna Janmashtami at Patan's Krishna Mandir. Marpha's apple season begins. Upper Mustang is good. Trekking south of the main range is slippery and cloudy, and road delays are common.
months.tip: Check road status on the Beni–Jomsom route before booking a jeep.

months.summary: The monsoon usually withdraws in the second half of September, and the skies begin to clear. Indra Jatra brings the Kumari's chariot and masked Lakhey dancers to Kathmandu Durbar Square. From late September Lukla flights move to Ramechhap again for the autumn rush. Early-month trails are still wet; by the last week, trekking season is open and Pokhara is green and bright.
months.tip: Stay near Kathmandu Durbar Square for the Indra Jatra evenings.

months.summary: October is Nepal's best and busiest month. The air is washed clean after the monsoon, the Annapurnas and Everest are clear from dawn to afternoon, and every major trail is open. Dashain, Nepal's biggest festival, usually falls in late September or October, followed by Tihar; buses fill as people go home and some offices close for days. Book flights, Lukla seats and teahouses well ahead.
months.tip: Avoid travelling by bus on the main Dashain travel days; seats sell out and fares rise.

months.summary: November keeps October's clear skies with fewer crowds by the end of the month. Nights are cold above 3,500 m, and Mani Rimdu is held at Tengboche in October or November by the Tibetan calendar. Poon Hill sunrises are reliably clear, Nagarkot shows the long line of peaks, and Upper Mustang is crisp but closing down by late November.
months.tip: From mid-November carry a warm sleeping bag rated to −10 °C for any trek above 4,000 m.

months.summary: December is cold and very clear. It suits the Kathmandu valley, Bandipur, Pokhara and Poon Hill, where the views are often the best of the year and the trails quiet. Everest Base Camp is possible for well-equipped trekkers, but nights fall well below freezing and some high lodges close. Year-end holidays bring Indian families to Pokhara and Nagarkot.
months.tip: Book Pokhara lakeside rooms early for the Christmas–New Year week.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a visa or passport for Nepal?
faqs.a: No visa is needed. Indian citizens can enter with a valid passport or a voter ID card issued by the Election Commission of India. Aadhaar and PAN cards are not accepted for adults; Aadhaar has been allowed for travellers under 15 and over 65. Children may need a birth certificate or school ID. Airlines check documents strictly, so carry your passport if you have one. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I use Indian rupees in Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes, widely. Indian ₹100 and smaller notes are accepted in most shops, hotels and bus counters, at the fixed rate of 1 INR = 1.6 NPR. After 2016 larger INR notes were banned in Nepal; in 2026 Nepal Rastra Bank allowed post-2016 ₹200 and ₹500 notes up to ₹25,000 per person. Many small shops still prefer ₹100s, and change comes in NPR. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Nepal trip cost from India?
faqs.a: A saver week by road from Gorakhpur via Sunauli, using buses and budget hotels, costs about ₹18,000–25,000 per person. A Poon Hill teahouse trek adds ₹3,000–4,500 a day including a shared guide. Everest Base Camp is ₹95,000–1,10,000 because of Lukla flights. Comfort trips with a car and good hotels run ₹7,000–12,000 a day, and signature trips ₹25,000–45,000 a day.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Nepal?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest mountain views and the most stable trekking weather. March and April are the second-best window, with rhododendron flowers but more haze. December to February suit the Kathmandu valley, Pokhara and low treks. June to September is monsoon: avoid treks south of the main range, but Upper Mustang and the Jomsom–Marpha valley are at their best then.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to trek in Nepal?
faqs.a: Since 1 April 2023 Nepal's rule is that foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas must trek with a licensed guide arranged through a registered agency. The Khumbu municipality around Everest has not applied it, so independent trekking there has continued. How checkposts apply the rule to Indian trekkers has varied, and restricted areas like Upper Mustang always need a guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I avoid altitude sickness in Nepal?
faqs.a: Above 3,000 m, raise your sleeping altitude by no more than 300–500 m a night and take a rest day every 1,000 m. On the Everest trail that means two nights at Namche and two at Dingboche. Drink 3–4 litres of water, skip alcohol early, and descend if headache, vomiting or breathlessness at rest get worse. Talk to your doctor about acetazolamide before you go.

faqs.q: Is Nepal safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Nepal is one of the easier Himalayan countries for women travelling alone. Thamel and Lakeside Pokhara are used to solo travellers, and hostels such as Zostel Kathmandu have female dorms. On treks, use a licensed guide from a registered agency, share a room only with people you know, and tell your lodge your plans. Avoid walking alone late at night in city back lanes.

faqs.q: Do Indian SIMs and UPI work in Nepal?
faqs.a: Indian roaming is expensive and not included in many prepaid plans, so most travellers buy a Nepal Telecom or Ncell SIM with a passport and photo. Data is good in cities and on main trek routes up to Namche and Ghorepani. UPI payments to Nepali merchants work at many larger shops through tie-ups between NPCI and Nepali payment networks, but carry cash for teahouses.

faqs.q: Can I drive my own car from India to Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes. At the border customs office you get a vehicle permit called a bhansar, paid per day, plus your registration, licence, insurance and pollution papers. Indian cars are common on the Sunauli–Pokhara and Raxaul–Kathmandu roads. Mountain roads are narrow, and the Kathmandu–Pokhara highway has long construction stretches. Upper Mustang and some park roads have their own rules. Check current status before you travel.
